rv.q: The playwright has reduced his components to the bare minimum, offering us Hunter superfans a chance to marvel at his elegant way with exposition and the stealthy way he lures us down into the deep end of the emotional pool.
Both are on exemplary view in this play, easily one of the best of the year.

“A Case for the Existence of God,” which opened on Monday in a Signature Theater production directed exquisitely by David Cromer, is another of Hunter’s public explorations of his own private Idaho: a post-boom, existential vastness in which emotional and economic collapse are conjoined.
Playgoers looking for a thought-provoking evening of theater will do well to consider Hunter’s compelling Case for the Existence of God.

Sublimely directed by David Cromer with the dignity and consequence of an instant classic, Samuel D. Hunter’s phenomenal new play brings the terror of such trapped existences to dizzying light with its two-man cast.
“A Case for the Existence of God” is a world premiere, and there hasn’t been a better one for a play this theater season in New York City.
In “A Case for the Existence of God,” they’ve done it again, this time together.
This devastating two-hander has a power all its own.
This 90-minute two-hander, which David Cromer directs, is one of the most moving new plays of the year.
The play is a case for a playwright at the height of his powers.

This beautifully designed production—including Brenda Abbandandolo’s subtly distinguished levels of contemporary casual, and Christopher Darbassie’s evocative sound effects—confronts us with a world at once naturalistic and epic in spiritual scale.
They are perfectly matched, and their every strained utterance and awkward gesture are completely believable.
The play is a beautifully observed character study in which we come to care deeply about these two men and their travails.
Some theatergoers may find it significant and enriching; others could find it synthetic and underwhelming.
The play ends with a surprise, a challenge for the actors and creative team alike, and it brings chills.

In fact, the play is more a case for the existence of humanism, the earthly miracle of two people finding connection amid a specific kind of sadness, and, at the end, perhaps even something resembling hope.

Luckily, Hunter has found an ideal collaborator in the brilliant director David Cromer, whose simple staging encourages us to focus on both Hunter’s words and Brill and Beltran’s finely calibrated performances.

cn.t: Hunter's quietly devastating two-hander about unlikely friendship between struggling Idaho fathers earns widespread praise for its empathetic writing and beautifully calibrated performances, though some find its modest scope underwhelming.
